domains.title: Python Foundations: From Values to Tested Programs
domains.description: An original, progressive Python 3.11+ course. Build a precise mental model, trace runnable examples, diagnose mistakes, and practice interview reasoning without replacing legacy Python material.

topics.title: Values, Types, and Name Binding
objectives: Distinguish an object from a name bound to it
Predict mutation versus rebinding
Use type, equality, and identity for different questions

content_blocks.value: Explanation: assignment is binding, not copying

A Python value is an object with a type, an identity, and a value. A name such as `scores` refers to an object; it is not a storage box containing a private copy. Assignment evaluates the right-hand expression first, then binds the left-hand name. An object has a type, but an ordinary name does not have a permanently declared type: rebinding can make it refer to another kind of object. This is dynamic typing, not an absence of types. Adding an integer to a string still raises TypeError unless you explicitly choose a conversion.

Mechanism: `backup = scores` creates a second binding to the same list. Calling append changes that list in place, so both bindings observe the change. Later, `scores = [90]` changes only the binding named scores. It does not reach into backup and redirect it. Lists are mutable; strings and integers are immutable. An operation on an immutable value computes a result rather than editing the original object. `==` asks about equality of values, while `is` asks whether two references identify exactly the same object.

content_blocks.title: Two names, one list, then a rebind
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Scores[scores before rebind] --> Shared[shared list]
    Backup[backup] --> Shared
    NewScores[scores after rebind] --> NewList[new list]
Worked example: keep an alias, then replace the working list

Before running the example, draw the two arrows after the second assignment. The first print follows the mutation through backup. The second follows the new scores binding. Finally a fresh list with equal contents compares equal, but it is not the same object. These are language-level observations; they do not rely on memory addresses or interpreter caching.

scores = [70, 80]
backup = scores
scores.append(85)
scores = [90]
print(backup)
print(scores)
print(backup == [70, 80, 85], backup is scores)
print(type(scores).__name__)

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: Do not use `is` to compare numbers or text: interning and caching can disguise the error. Use `is None` for the singleton sentinel. Aliasing is useful for deliberate shared state, but copying may be needed for independent state; a shallow copy does not isolate nested objects. Avoid saying assignment always creates an object: it may reuse an existing one.

content_blocks.question: After `items = [1]; alias = items; items = [2]`, what does alias contain?
content_blocks.explanation: Rebinding items does not change alias. Alias still refers to the original list containing 1.

content_blocks.question: Two separately created lists contain the same integers. Which comparison asks whether their contents are equal?
content_blocks.explanation: List equality compares corresponding elements. Identity checks whether there is one shared object, not whether contents match.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: move append below the rebind and explain which printed list changes.
Modify: replace `backup = scores` with `backup = scores.copy()` and predict all four output lines before running.
Design: a caller gives your function a list of scores. State explicitly whether the function may mutate it, then choose aliasing or copying to honor that contract.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

Why can a function change a caller's list but not rebind the caller's local variable? A strong answer separates the shared object from the function's own parameter binding; it does not claim that lists are passed by reference while integers are passed by value.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-numeric-reasoning. Keep asking whether an expression converts, mutates, or simply produces a new value.

content_blocks.label: Python data model: objects, values, and types

topics.title: Numeric Reasoning and Precision
objectives: Trace floor division and remainder including negative operands
Separate binary approximation from decimal requirements
Choose explicit numeric conversions and comparison tolerances

content_blocks.value: Explanation: representation is part of correctness

Python integers support arbitrary precision, subject to available memory. `/` performs true division; integer operands normally produce a float. `//` produces a floored quotient, and `%` produces the corresponding remainder. With integer operands and a nonzero divisor, `total == (total // size) * size + total % size`. Flooring is toward negative infinity, not toward zero: -7 // 3 is -3 and -7 % 3 is 2. This matters for bucketing coordinates or decomposing a duration, not just for arithmetic quizzes.

Mechanism: most Python floats store finite binary fractions. Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly, so rounding enters before a later addition or comparison. Use `math.isclose` when a measured quantity has a meaningful tolerance; near zero, an absolute tolerance may be necessary. For decimal amounts use Decimal constructed from strings, and specify rounding rules when required. Decimal still has a precision context and is not unlimited exact arithmetic for every operation. Formatting a float to two digits changes its display, not its stored value.

content_blocks.title: Choose representation from the requirement
content_blocks.value:
flowchart TD
    Meaning[Numeric requirement] --> Count[Exact integer count]
    Meaning --> Measure[Approximate measurement]
    Meaning --> Money[Decimal amount]
    Count --> Integer[int]
    Measure --> Float[float and tolerance]
    Money --> Decimal[Decimal from text]
Worked example: crates, negative offsets, and a price

Seventeen items fill three crates of five with two left over. A negative offset illustrates why floor division cannot be replaced by truncation. The measurement comparison tolerates a small representation difference, while the price calculation starts from exact decimal strings. Notice that the example tests the numeric meaning rather than depending on a long, implementation-sensitive float display.

from decimal import Decimal
from math import isclose

print(divmod(17, 5))
print(-7 // 3, -7 % 3)
print(isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, abs_tol=1e-12))
price = Decimal('0.10') + Decimal('0.20')
print(price)

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: `int(-2.9)` truncates to -2, unlike floor division's direction. `Decimal(0.1)` imports the float approximation; start from '0.1' instead. Decimal adds cost and does not choose a business rounding policy for you. A fixed epsilon is not automatically suitable for quantities with different units or magnitudes.

content_blocks.question: What is -8 // 3?
content_blocks.explanation: The exact quotient is between -3 and -2. Flooring toward negative infinity gives -3.

content_blocks.question: Which starts Decimal from the intended decimal tenth without importing a binary float approximation?
content_blocks.explanation: The string supplies a decimal representation directly. The float constructor receives an already approximated binary value.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: calculate divmod(-8, 3) and verify the quotient-remainder identity by hand.
Modify: calculate the cost of seven items priced at Decimal('1.25'), then display a two-decimal result.
Design: compare two sensor readings close to zero. State the units and acceptable absolute error before choosing abs_tol; include exact equality and clearly different readings as cases.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

Why can rounding the displayed result fail to repair a monetary algorithm? Explain the difference between representation, intermediate calculations, and display. Discuss integer minor units for fixed-scale amounts versus Decimal for variable decimal arithmetic.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-text-and-unicode to see why parsing and formatting are separate from the underlying value.

topics.title: Text, Unicode, and Explicit Encoding
objectives: Distinguish Unicode strings from encoded bytes
Use slicing and string methods without expecting mutation
Separate normalization, parsing, and output formatting

subtopics.title: Text is not its byte representation

content_blocks.value: Explanation: characters inside, bytes at boundaries

A `str` represents Unicode text and is immutable. Indexing selects a code point as another string; slicing selects a half-open range. String methods return new strings, so `name.strip()` alone does not change name. A `bytes` object represents byte values, not already-decoded text. Encode when sending text to a byte-oriented interface and decode when receiving bytes, choosing an encoding explicitly. UTF-8 can use multiple bytes for one code point, so the number of bytes and len(text) can differ.

Mechanism: the example first strips boundary whitespace, then casefolds for a caseless comparison key. Casefolding is not identical to lowercasing and can expand some characters. Encoding maps the Unicode string to UTF-8 bytes; decoding reverses that mapping when the data and encoding are valid. Do not infer human-visible character count from len alone: a displayed symbol can contain several code points. Formatting with an f-string creates presentation text; it does not turn a number into a more precise numeric value.

content_blocks.title: An explicit text boundary
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Raw[Incoming UTF-8 bytes] --> Decode[Decode]
    Decode --> Text[Unicode string]
    Text --> Normalize[Strip and casefold]
    Normalize --> Encode[Encode UTF-8]
    Encode --> Bytes[Outgoing bytes]
Worked example: a normalized display key

The input includes surrounding spaces and a non-ASCII letter. The normalized key contains four code points but encodes to five UTF-8 bytes. The slice starts at position one and stops before three. A round trip returns the original normalized text because both directions use the same encoding. The final line presents a numeric score to one decimal place without changing the score itself.

raw_name = '  Café  '
key = raw_name.strip().casefold()
payload = key.encode('utf-8')
print(key)
print(len(key), len(payload))
print(key[1:3])
print(payload.decode('utf-8') == key)
score = 8.25
print(f'{key}: {score:.1f}')

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: Do not write `str(payload)` expecting decoding: that produces a representation of the bytes. Splitting with no separator collapses whitespace, but splitting with ',' preserves empty fields; choose based on your format. Casefolding is a search policy, not a reason to overwrite someone's display name. Unicode normalization is a separate concern from casefolding.

content_blocks.question: After `name = ' Ada '; name.strip()`, what is name?
content_blocks.explanation: strip returns a new string. The original binding is unchanged unless you assign the result.

content_blocks.question: Which converts known UTF-8 bytes into Unicode text?
content_blocks.explanation: decode interprets bytes using an encoding. str(bytes) gives a representation, and bytes do not use str.encode for this conversion.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: compare 'a,,b'.split(',') with 'a  b'.split(). Count the fields in each result.
Modify: retain raw_name for display while deriving a separate normalized lookup key. Demonstrate that neither string is mutated.

Design: accept a UTF-8 byte payload containing comma-separated tags. Decode once, reject decoding failures, strip each field, and state whether blank tags should be kept. Avoid treating split as a full CSV parser.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

Why can a length check on a string disagree with a network payload-size limit? Explain code points versus encoded bytes. Also explain why neither count necessarily equals the number of visible characters a user perceives.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-conditions-and-truth. Normalized values still need explicit validation rules.

topics.title: Conditions, Truthiness, and Short-Circuiting
objectives: Distinguish absence from valid falsy values
Trace operand-returning and/or expressions
Write ordered conditions with explicit boundaries

content_blocks.value: Explanation: falsy does not necessarily mean missing

An if statement selects a suite according to a truth test. Empty containers, empty strings, zero, False, and None are common falsy values. The language groups them for branching, but your domain may need to distinguish them: a timeout of zero can mean 'do not wait', whereas None can mean 'use the default'. `if value is None` tests this absence policy precisely. In an if/elif chain only the first satisfied branch runs; arrange overlapping conditions intentionally and test their boundary values.

Mechanism: `left and right` evaluates left first. If left is falsy it returns left without evaluating right; otherwise it returns right. `left or right` returns left when left is truthy, otherwise evaluates and returns right. These operators select operands and do not promise a bool result. Short-circuiting can protect an operation, for example checking a divisor before dividing. A chained comparison such as `0 <= score <= 100` states an interval and evaluates the middle expression once.

content_blocks.title: Preserve zero when supplying a default
content_blocks.value:
flowchart TD
    Input[timeout value] --> Missing{Is None?}
    Missing -->|yes| Default[Use 30]
    Missing -->|no| Preserve[Keep supplied value]
    Default --> Result[Effective timeout]
    Preserve --> Result
Worked example: a timeout and a guarded division

The first defaulting expression preserves zero, while the or expression discards it. In the guarded comparison the denominator is zero, so the division is not evaluated at all. A final grade boundary uses a chained comparison and converts the result to an explicit label. Trace which expression executes, not just which final value prints.

configured_timeout = 0
effective_timeout = 30 if configured_timeout is None else configured_timeout
print(effective_timeout, configured_timeout or 30)
denominator = 0
print(denominator != 0 and 10 / denominator > 2)
print('ready' and 7)
score = 100
print('valid' if 0 <= score <= 100 else 'invalid')

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: `value == 'yes' or 'y'` is always truthy because 'y' is a nonempty string. Use membership in a collection of accepted values. Avoid complicated boolean expressions that hide several side effects; explicit branches are easier to review. Validate that a value has the expected type before making numeric comparisons.

content_blocks.question: A supplied zero must be preserved. Which test identifies only the missing sentinel?
content_blocks.explanation: is None distinguishes the absence sentinel from zero, False, and empty containers.

content_blocks.question: What is the value of `'' or 'fallback'`?
content_blocks.explanation: The empty string is falsy, so or evaluates and returns the second operand rather than a Boolean conversion.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: evaluate None or 4, 0 and 4, and 'ok' and 4. Give the value and its type.
Modify: classify scores below 0, at 0, at 60, at 100, and above 100. Ensure invalid scores are rejected before pass/fail classification.
Design: build a configuration rule that preserves False and zero but defaults only for None. Write a truth table before choosing a conditional expression.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

When is `result = supplied or default` incorrect? Give a legitimate falsy input and contrast absence detection with general truth testing. Explain why short-circuiting can avoid an exception without turning every expression into a Boolean.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-loops-and-invariants to apply explicit conditions repeatedly while preserving a statement of correctness.

content_blocks.label: Truth value testing and Boolean operations

topics.title: Loops, Search, and Invariants
objectives: Trace a for loop as iteration over values
Explain loop else by the absence of break
Maintain an invariant and a termination argument

content_blocks.value: Explanation: an invariant connects iterations

A for loop asks an iterable for successive values rather than maintaining a hidden C-style numeric counter. Use enumerate when both a position and a value matter. range supplies a half-open arithmetic progression: its stop value is excluded. A while loop repeats while its condition stays true, so you must also explain how progress eventually makes that condition false. An invariant is a statement true before and after each iteration; it gives meaning to the accumulated state instead of leaving correctness to a few successful examples.

Mechanism: in a search for the first negative reading, every completed iteration without break establishes that all inspected readings are nonnegative. When a negative value appears, its current index is the first match because the earlier prefix has already been ruled out. `break` exits the loop and suppresses the loop's else suite. On normal exhaustion, else runs, including for an empty iterable. `continue` skips the remainder of one iteration but does not itself suppress else. An exception is not normal exhaustion and does not trigger else.

content_blocks.title: Search with a first-match invariant

content_blocks.value: Worked example: find a fault and count accepted readings

The search visits 4, then 7, then -2 and stops at index two. In the second loop, accepted equals the count of nonnegative values in the prefix processed so far. Continue excludes negatives from that count. Finally the empty loop demonstrates that else does not mean 'the loop ran at least once'. Each loop has a different state contract even though they share the same input.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: Removing list items during forward iteration can skip shifted elements. Build a filtered result or iterate a deliberate copy. A for loop is clearer for finite input; a while loop fits state-driven repetition but requires a progress condition. A linear search can stop early, yet still inspects every item in the no-match case.

content_blocks.question: A for loop has zero items and no exception. Does its else suite execute?
options: Yes, normal exhaustion occurs without break
No, else needs at least one iteration
content_blocks.explanation: Loop else runs after normal exhaustion without break. An empty iterable is exhausted immediately.

content_blocks.question: Before each iteration of the first-negative search, what has been established?
options: Every already inspected reading is nonnegative
content_blocks.explanation: If an earlier value were negative, the loop would already have broken. The uninspected suffix has no such guarantee.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: trace the search for an empty input, a first-item negative, and an all-positive input. Identify when else runs.
Modify: compute the sum of accepted readings. State the sum-over-prefix invariant and verify it after each iteration.
Design: return the first adjacent pair whose difference exceeds a threshold. Account for inputs of length zero and one; explain why your loop bounds never read beyond the end.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

How would you prove a running-total loop correct? Describe initialization, preservation by one iteration, and the meaning of the invariant at termination. Then separate that correctness argument from the loop's time and memory costs.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-functions-and-contracts. Turn a traced loop into a reusable operation with a clear return value and mutation policy.

topics.title: Functions, Arguments, and Contracts
objectives: Separate return values from printing and mutation
Explain definition-time defaults
Use parameter kinds to make caller intent explicit

subtopics.title: A reusable operation has a contract

content_blocks.value: Explanation: inputs, outputs, and side effects

A function contract says which inputs are accepted, which result is returned, and which observable state may change. Printing is an output side effect, not a returned value. Falling off the end returns None. Python binds parameter names to the argument objects: a function can mutate a supplied list, but rebinding its parameter does not replace a caller's variable. Small functions that return results are easier to compose and test than functions that silently combine parsing, mutation, and printing.

Mechanism: a def statement creates a function object and evaluates its default expressions at that time, not at every call. A default list would therefore be reused on calls that omit that argument. Use None as a sentinel and allocate inside the body when each call needs a fresh container. A `*` before a named parameter makes following parameters keyword-only. In the example, callers must spell out include_boundary, avoiding an unexplained positional True at the call site. Return finishes the call immediately with the selected result.

content_blocks.title: Separate a pure result from shared state
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Caller[Argument objects] --> Bind[Bind local parameters]
    Bind --> Compute[Compute fresh result]
    Compute --> Return[Return result]
    Bind --> Mutate[Optional declared mutation]
    Mutate --> Caller
Worked example: a boundary policy and independent log defaults

The filter returns a new list and leaves readings untouched. Its keyword-only flag chooses whether zero is acceptable. The event helper creates a new list only when no list is supplied; when a caller supplies one, the documented contract permits mutation. Two calls with omitted events therefore cannot leak state into each other. This distinction is intentional, not a universal instruction to copy every argument.

def accepted_readings(readings, *, include_boundary=False):
    return [reading for reading in readings if reading > 0 or (include_boundary and reading == 0)]

def record_event(event, events=None):
    if events is None:
        events = []
    events.append(event)
    return events

readings = [-1, 0, 2]
print(accepted_readings(readings, include_boundary=True))
print(readings)
print(record_event('start'))
print(record_event('stop'))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: Using list() instead of [] as a default still evaluates once. Returning `items.append(value)` returns None because append mutates rather than producing the list. Keyword-only flags improve readability but cannot repair a vague contract. The sentinel approach should preserve an explicitly supplied empty list, so test `is None`, not `if not events`.

content_blocks.question: When is the default list in `def collect(items=[]): ...` evaluated?
options: Only when the first item is added
content_blocks.explanation: Default objects are established at function definition time and reused by calls that omit the corresponding argument.

content_blocks.question: A function only calls print and reaches its end. What does the caller receive?
content_blocks.explanation: Printing writes to stdout. Without an explicit return value, the call result is None.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: call record_event twice using the same explicit list. Explain why this differs from two omitted-default calls.
Modify: make accepted_readings reject a negative threshold and expose the threshold as a keyword-only parameter.
Design: implement summarize_scores that returns a count and total without printing or mutating input. Document the empty-input result and test it separately from display code.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

What does 'Python passes objects by sharing' explain about both lists and integers? Use the same binding model for both. Then describe why mutable defaults produce persistent state and why a fresh local allocation solves that particular problem.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-scope-and-closures. Function parameters are local bindings, but nested functions can retain enclosing state.

topics.title: Scope, Closures, and Late Binding
objectives: Trace local and enclosing name resolution
Use nonlocal for deliberate enclosing rebinding
Diagnose closure late binding without treating it as copying

subtopics.title: A function remembers bindings, not snapshots

content_blocks.value: Explanation: scope is determined by code structure

For ordinary function code, name lookup searches local, enclosing function, module global, and built-in namespaces. Assignment normally makes a name local throughout that function body, unless global or nonlocal says otherwise. Reading such a local before it has a value raises UnboundLocalError even if a same-named global exists. This lexical rule is based on the code, not on which caller invoked the function. Class bodies and newer language constructs have additional scope rules, so the familiar lookup mnemonic is a useful model, not the entire specification.

Mechanism: a closure retains access to bindings from an enclosing function after that outer call returns. In a counter factory, each factory invocation creates its own state. The nested function declares nonlocal to rebind the nearest enclosing count rather than introducing a new local. A loop that constructs several lambdas over the same loop binding does not freeze each value: calling later reads the final binding. A default parameter such as `offset=offset` captures the current object at definition time when that is the intended behavior.

content_blocks.title: Independent closure state
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Factory[Counter factory] --> First[First enclosing count]
    Factory --> Second[Second enclosing count]
    CallA[First returned function] --> First
    CallB[Second returned function] --> Second
Worked example: two counters and captured offsets

The first counter advances twice while the second advances once from its independent initial state. The offset defaults are evaluated as each lambda is created, so these functions return distinct values. Remove the default and all lambdas instead consult the same final comprehension-loop binding. Trace the lifetime of the binding rather than imagining that the lambda's source text substitutes a number.

def make_counter(start):
    count = start
    def advance():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return advance

first = make_counter(10)
second = make_counter(10)
print(first(), first(), second())
steps = [lambda offset=offset: offset for offset in range(3)]
print([step() for step in steps])

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: nonlocal requires an existing enclosing function binding; it does not target arbitrary globals. Mutating an enclosing list does not require nonlocal, but rebinding that list name does. Closures offer compact private state, while a class is often clearer when state has several operations or needs inspection. Capturing a mutable default captures an object, not a deep snapshot.

content_blocks.question: A function reads count and later assigns count without nonlocal/global. A global count exists. What can the early read raise?
options: No error because the global wins
content_blocks.explanation: Assignment makes count local to that function body. The early read occurs before the local binding has a value.

content_blocks.question: After `jobs = [lambda: offset for offset in range(3)]`, what do all three jobs return when called later?
content_blocks.explanation: The closures share the comprehension's offset binding and read its final value, 2, at call time.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: create three counters with different starts, interleave calls, and track three independent counts.
Modify: add a step parameter to make_counter and retain it read-only in the closure. Identify which name actually needs nonlocal.
Design: create callbacks that label distinct menu positions. Demonstrate the late-binding failure, then fix it with defaults or a factory and explain the tradeoff.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

Why do loop-created callbacks often report the final loop value? Explain retained bindings and call-time lookup, then distinguish a captured immutable value from a captured mutable object that can still change.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-sequences-and-copying, where nested containers make shared references visible again.

topics.title: Sequences, Aliasing, and Copy Depth
objectives: Trace nested references through shallow copies
Choose lists and tuples by their contracts
Build independent nested rows without accidental aliasing

content_blocks.value: Explanation: copying the outside is not copying the inside

Lists are mutable sequences; tuples keep their element references fixed after construction. Both support indexing and half-open slicing. A list slice or list.copy creates a new outer list whose elements still refer to the original element objects. If those elements are lists, mutations can be visible through both outer containers. Tuple immutability also does not freeze an embedded list. A tuple can represent a fixed record shape while the referenced objects still have their own mutability contracts.

Mechanism: `[[0, 0]] * 2` repeats a reference to one inner row, not the operation that creates a row. Assigning a cell in one displayed row therefore changes the shared row seen at both positions. A comprehension evaluating a row expression for every iteration creates independent rows. A shallow outer copy is sufficient when elements are immutable or intentionally shared; recursive deepcopy can isolate more state, but it has cost and must respect objects with special copy behavior. Ask what independence the caller actually needs.

content_blocks.title: Shallow copy keeps the inner row shared
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Original[Original outer list] --> Row[Shared inner row]
    Copy[Shallow outer copy] --> Row
    Independent[Fresh outer list] --> NewRow[Fresh inner row]
Worked example: shared rows versus independent rows

The repeated-row matrix has a single row object, so one cell assignment appears twice. A row-by-row copy creates fresh inner lists and leaves its source untouched. The final tuple contains a list; the tuple still refers to the same list after append, demonstrating that immutable container structure does not mean recursive immutability. These examples use explicit values instead of interpreter-specific object sizes.

shared_rows = [[0, 0]] * 2
shared_rows[0][1] = 5
print(shared_rows)
original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
independent = [row.copy() for row in original]
independent[0][0] = 9
print(original)
print(independent)
record = ('Ada', [80])
record[1].append(90)
print(record)

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: Calling a copy 'deep' because the outer id changed misses nested references. Row-by-row copying here handles a two-level list of integers, not an arbitrary object graph. CPython lists commonly provide amortized constant-time append, but insertion near the front shifts references. For frequent removal from the front, consider collections.deque rather than repeatedly using pop(0).

content_blocks.question: After `original = [[1]]; copied = original.copy(); copied[0].append(2)`, what is original?
content_blocks.explanation: The outer list was copied but its inner list remains shared. append changes that shared inner list.

content_blocks.question: Which operation is allowed for `record = ('Ada', [])`?
content_blocks.explanation: The tuple's slots cannot be replaced, but its second slot refers to a mutable list whose append operation remains available.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: replace independent with original.copy() and redraw the shared-reference diagram before computing outputs.
Modify: create a three-by-two zero matrix with independent rows, change one cell, and confirm exactly one position changes.

Design: accept a matrix of integers and return a version with one edited cell without modifying the input. Explain why a two-level copy is sufficient for that input contract, then describe what changes for cells containing mutable objects.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

Why is tuple immutability not sufficient to guarantee hashability? A good answer notes that every element must be hashable; a tuple containing a list fails even though its own slots cannot be reassigned. Connect this to the upcoming mapping lesson.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-mappings-and-sets to choose containers for lookup and uniqueness, not just position.

topics.title: Mappings, Sets, and Hash Contracts
objectives: Choose dictionary lookup versus sequence search
Explain hashability and equality requirements
Preserve input order while removing duplicates

subtopics.title: Lookup needs a stable key contract

content_blocks.value: Explanation: association and uniqueness are different jobs

A dict maps unique keys to values; a set stores distinct elements for membership and set operations. Keys and set elements must be hashable. A hash must remain stable during the object's lifetime, and objects that compare equal must have equal hashes. Lists and dicts are unhashable; a tuple is hashable only when every element is hashable. Immutability is not a complete synonym for hashability: user-defined objects can have identity-based hashes even when attributes are mutable.

Mechanism: hash-based lookup narrows candidate positions and equality distinguishes keys, including after hash collisions. Typical dictionary and set membership is fast on average, not guaranteed constant time in every circumstance. Python dictionaries preserve insertion order as a language guarantee from 3.7 onward. Reassigning an existing key changes its value without moving its insertion position. Sets do not promise the same iteration order. To deduplicate while preserving first occurrence, use a seen set for membership and a separate output list for order.

content_blocks.title: Stable first-seen deduplication
content_blocks.value:
flowchart TD
    Word[Next normalized word] --> Seen{Already in seen set?}
    Seen -->|yes| Skip[Skip duplicate]
    Seen -->|no| Add[Add to seen and output list]
    Skip --> Word
    Add --> Word
Worked example: first-seen labels and ordered counts

The seen set answers only the membership question, while unique_labels records first occurrence. The dictionary tracks counts in the same first-seen order. At the end, updating red's count leaves red before blue. A missing-key get returns the supplied default without creating an entry. This distinction matters when you want a read to remain side-effect-free.

labels = ['red', 'blue', 'red', 'green']
seen = set()
unique_labels = []
counts = {}
for label in labels:
    counts[label] = counts.get(label, 0) + 1
    if label not in seen:
        seen.add(label)
        unique_labels.append(label)
print(unique_labels)
print(list(counts.items()))
counts['red'] = 9
print(list(counts))
print(counts.get('orange', 0), 'orange' in counts)

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: Do not sort a set merely to claim you preserved input order: sorting imposes a different order. `key in mapping` tests keys, not values. `get` can blur missing versus a stored None unless you use membership or a distinct sentinel. A set uses additional memory; for very small inputs a list scan may be adequate. Never derive stable output from set iteration order.

content_blocks.question: Which built-in value is hashable and suitable as a dictionary key?
content_blocks.explanation: The last tuple contains only hashable elements. Lists are unhashable, including when nested inside a tuple.

content_blocks.question: In `counts = {'red': 1, 'blue': 2}`, assigning counts['red'] = 3 does what to key order?
content_blocks.explanation: Updating an existing key changes its value but does not change its insertion position.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: delete red from counts and insert it again. Compare that order change with a simple value update.
Modify: normalize labels with strip and casefold before counting while retaining the first display spelling separately.
Design: return the first repeated label and its position. Use a seen set, handle no repeats, and explain average lookup cost and the extra-memory requirement.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

What must be true of hashes when two keys compare equal, and why is a constant hash legal but potentially slow? Separate correctness of the equality/hash contract from collision-related performance. Avoid claiming that hash values are unique identifiers.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-comprehensions-and-sorting to express transformations while keeping ordering requirements explicit.

topics.title: Comprehensions and Stable Ranking
objectives: Trace filter and transformation order in a comprehension
Use sort keys to state ranking rules
Explain stable ties and sort versus sorted

subtopics.title: Transform data with an explicit order policy

content_blocks.value: Explanation: concise syntax still needs a contract

A list comprehension builds a fresh list by visiting input items, testing any filter, and evaluating the result expression for accepted items. The trailing if filters elements; a conditional expression before for chooses between two output values and does not remove an element. Set comprehensions remove duplicates, and dict comprehensions associate keys with values, so repeated keys replace earlier values. Comprehensions are useful for direct transformations; complex validation, exception handling, or several side effects are usually clearer as a loop.

Mechanism: sorted creates a new list from an iterable; list.sort rearranges that list in place and returns None. A key function computes a comparison key once for each item. Python's sort is stable: items with equal keys retain their relative input order. Tuple keys compare lexicographically, letting you express primary and secondary criteria. For descending numeric scores but ascending names, use `(-score, name)` rather than reversing the entire tuple order. Choose a tie policy deliberately instead of treating incidental input order as a ranking specification.

content_blocks.title: A ranking pipeline
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Input[Input records] --> Filter[Keep valid scores]
    Filter --> Key[Compute ranking key]
    Key --> Sort[Stable sort]
    Sort --> Output[Ranked display records]
Worked example: rank valid candidates two ways

Filtering removes the negative score. The score-only key preserves the original order of the tied 90-point candidates: Mira stays before Ada. Adding name as a secondary key intentionally reverses that tie. The original records remain unchanged because sorted creates new lists. This provides a concrete check that the algorithm's tie policy and mutation contract are both correct.

records = [('Mira', 90), ('Ada', 90), ('Lin', 75), ('Noor', -1)]
valid = [record for record in records if record[1] >= 0]
stable = sorted(valid, key=lambda record: -record[1])
named = sorted(valid, key=lambda record: (-record[1], record[0]))
print([name for name, score in stable])
print([name for name, score in named])
print(len(records), len(valid))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: `ranked = valid.sort()` sets ranked to None. reverse=True reverses every component of a tuple-key ordering, not only the score. A sorted result allocates a new list; in-place sorting saves that result allocation but changes shared state. Nested comprehensions can be correct yet harder to audit than a short named function and explicit loop.

content_blocks.question: What does `[number * 2 for number in [0, 1, 2] if number > 0]` produce?
content_blocks.explanation: The filter rejects zero, then the expression doubles the two accepted inputs.

content_blocks.question: A stable sort sees two records with equal keys. What happens to their relative order?
options: It follows their original input order
content_blocks.explanation: Stability preserves the input order of equal-key items; secondary ordering requires an explicit secondary key.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: change the trailing filter to a conditional output expression and explain why the output count changes.
Modify: rank records by descending score and ascending casefolded name, preserving order when both keys match.
Design: a two-stage report first groups by department and then ranks by score. Compare a tuple-key sort with two stable sorts applied from secondary to primary criterion; verify ties explicitly.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

How can stable sorting express multiple criteria without a custom comparator? Discuss tuple keys and the order of multiple sort passes. Include the non-mutation difference between sorted and list.sort, not only the final ordering.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-iterators-and-generators to avoid materializing every intermediate list when a one-pass stream is enough.

topics.title: Iterators, Generators, and Consumption
objectives: Distinguish iterable containers from one-shot iterators
Trace suspension and resumption at yield
Choose lazy streaming or materialization from consumption needs

content_blocks.value: Explanation: iteration is a protocol, not a list

An iterable can supply an iterator through iter(). An iterator supplies successive values through next() and signals completion with StopIteration. Lists are reusable iterables: requesting a new iterator starts a new traversal. An iterator normally retains a consumption position and returns itself from iter(), so a second loop over the same exhausted iterator finds no items. `next(iterator, default)` supplies a default on exhaustion instead of raising. Do not confuse an empty stream with a stream whose first valid value is None.

Mechanism: calling a generator function returns a generator object without running its body. The first next begins execution; yield produces one value and suspends the function's local state. The next request resumes after that yield. Finishing the function ends the iterator. A generator expression similarly computes its result values on demand, although its outermost iterable expression is evaluated immediately. Streaming can reduce intermediate storage for a one-pass reduction, but does not guarantee that the input source itself occupies constant memory or that the computation is faster.

content_blocks.title: Suspended generator state
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Created[Generator created] --> Request[next requested]
    Request --> Running[Run until yield]
    Running --> Suspended[Return value and suspend]
    Suspended --> Request
    Running --> Exhausted[Return ends iteration]
Worked example: partial consumption is observable

The first next consumes only the first matching square. list then consumes the remaining matches, and a subsequent list is empty. A fresh factory call starts a new independent traversal for sum. The explicit iterator demonstrates a default after exhaustion. If you need both a count and a total, a single reduction may be preferable to attempting two passes over one stream.

def positive_squares(values):
    for value in values:
        if value > 0:
            yield value * value

stream = positive_squares([-1, 2, 3])
print(next(stream))
print(list(stream))
print(list(stream))
print(sum(positive_squares([-1, 2, 3])))
iterator = iter([5])
print(next(iterator, 'done'), next(iterator, 'done'))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: `if stream` does not tell you whether a generator has remaining values; a generator object is truthy even when exhausted. Materialize when you need random access or repeated traversal and the data fits memory. Deferred work can also defer errors and hold resources longer. Keep file iteration inside its resource lifetime rather than returning a stream tied to a closed handle.

content_blocks.question: After `stream = iter([2, 3]); list(stream)`, what does a second list(stream) produce?
content_blocks.explanation: The first list consumes both values. The same iterator is exhausted and cannot restart itself.

content_blocks.question: When does the body of a generator function first begin executing?
options: When the generator function is called
When its first item is requested
content_blocks.explanation: Calling creates the generator object. A next request or equivalent iteration begins the body and runs toward the first yield.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: consume one element with next, then use sum, then list. Track the consumption position after each operation.
Modify: yield running totals rather than squares. Keep only the running accumulator and explain when the first value is computed.
Design: compute count and total of positive readings in a single traversal over an iterator. Handle no accepted values without a second pass or an unnecessary list.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

Why can replacing a list with a generator break a previously correct two-pass algorithm? Explain exhaustion, deferred execution, and resource lifetime. Give one case where materialization is the more honest and maintainable choice.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-exceptions-and-boundaries. Deferred work may fail at consumption time, so exception boundaries must enclose the actual operation.

topics.title: Exceptions and Validation Boundaries
objectives: Catch expected failures without hiding programming errors
Distinguish conversion errors from domain validation errors
Use else, finally, and exception chaining intentionally

content_blocks.value: Explanation: an exception marks a failed operation

An exception interrupts ordinary control flow and searches outward for a matching handler. Match specific expected types close to the operation you know how to recover from. Invalid decimal text passed to int raises ValueError; a syntactically valid negative count can instead fail your domain rule. Both failures need an explicit policy rather than silently substituting zero. A broad except Exception can obscure a typo or broken invariant. BaseException also includes interruption-oriented exceptions that ordinary application recovery usually should not swallow.

Mechanism: the try suite contains the risky operation. A matching except handles its exception; else runs only when the try suite completes without an exception, keeping unrelated follow-up code out of the handler's scope. finally runs as control leaves the construct, including on return or exception, but a return inside finally can suppress an earlier result or error. `raise NewError(...) from original` retains a causal chain when translating an implementation error into a domain-specific failure. Resource cleanup is often clearer with a context manager.

content_blocks.title: Parse, validate, then use
content_blocks.value:
flowchart TD
    Text[Input text] --> Parse[Convert to integer]
    Parse -->|ValueError| Reject[Reject invalid syntax]
    Parse --> Validate{Nonnegative?}
    Validate -->|no| Domain[Reject invalid count]
    Validate -->|yes| Use[Use valid value]
Worked example: two distinct reasons to reject a count

The helper translates a conversion error to a clearer ValueError while preserving the cause, then checks the nonnegative rule separately. The caller catches the intended domain failure and prints a stable message. Its else prints success only for the valid input. The example never depends on platform-specific traceback formatting, and a programming error outside ValueError would not be silently converted into a valid count.

content_blocks.expected_output:
accepted: 4
invalid: count must be integer text
invalid: count must be nonnegative

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: assert is for internal checks, not validation of external input: optimized Python can remove assertions. Do not put a large computation inside a try intended only for parsing. Recovering per record can keep a batch moving, but may require reporting rejected records; aborting the whole batch can better preserve an all-or-nothing contract. State which policy you choose.

content_blocks.question: When does a try statement's else suite run?
options: When the try suite completes without an exception
content_blocks.explanation: else is the success path for the try suite. An exception handled by except does not enter else.

content_blocks.question: Why should assert not enforce that an external count is nonnegative?
options: Assertions can be omitted in optimized execution
content_blocks.explanation: Optimization can remove assert statements. External input validation must use ordinary checks and deliberate failures.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: classify '0', '-0', '3.5', and ' 8 ' under the helper's actual conversion and domain rules.
Modify: return a record containing the original text and the failure reason for rejected values, without catching unrelated error types.
Design: process a batch of count strings with both strict and tolerant modes. Specify whether valid results survive a later failure, and test that policy with a mixed batch.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

How can a broad exception handler make a service appear healthy while returning wrong results? Show the distinction between expected invalid input and an implementation defect, then explain what preserving an exception cause adds to diagnosis.

content_blocks.title: Next step
content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-files-and-json. File access, decoding, parsing, and application validation are separate failure boundaries.

topics.title: Files, Context Managers, and JSON Validation
objectives: Bound resource lifetime with a context manager
Separate JSON syntax from application schema
Choose explicit encoding and safe file-write semantics

subtopics.title: A successful parse is not a validated record

content_blocks.value: Explanation: four boundaries before trusted data

Reading a structured text file involves resource access, byte decoding, syntax parsing, and schema validation. Passing one stage does not establish the next. A JSON array can contain a string where your application expects a mapping, or true where it expects an integer score. Python bool is a subclass of int, so a strict integer rule can deliberately use `type(score) is int` instead of isinstance. JSON object keys are text; arbitrary Python objects do not have a portable automatic JSON representation.

Mechanism: with opens a resource and invokes its cleanup protocol as the suite exits, including when an exception occurs. Specify UTF-8 for text rather than relying on a platform default. json.load reads from a handle, while json.loads parses a string. Validate the top-level shape before indexing records and validate each field before computing. The example uses a TemporaryDirectory, so its file stays inside an isolated temporary location and is removed afterward. In production, a write mode such as 'w' truncates an existing file; a context manager closes the handle but does not make a write atomic.

content_blocks.title: Layers of validation
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    File[File resource] --> Decode[UTF-8 text]
    Decode --> Parse[JSON syntax]
    Parse --> Shape[Record and field checks]
    Shape --> Compute[Trusted computation]
Worked example: a safe temporary report

The authored records are serialized to a temporary UTF-8 file and read back before use. Each score must be exactly an int and in range, excluding booleans even though ordinary numeric comparisons would accept them. The program prints a deterministic summary rather than a random temporary path. It reads while the directory still exists and closes each handle before the directory context removes its files.

import json
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / 'scores.json'
    records = [{'name': 'Ada', 'score': 80}, {'name': 'Lin', 'score': 90}]
    with path.open('w', encoding='utf-8') as handle:
        json.dump(records, handle)
    with path.open(encoding='utf-8') as handle:
        loaded = json.load(handle)
    if not isinstance(loaded, list):
        raise ValueError('expected a list')
    for record in loaded:
        if not isinstance(record, dict):
            raise ValueError('expected a record')
        score = record.get('score')
        if type(score) is not int or not 0 <= score <= 100:
            raise ValueError('invalid score')
    print(len(loaded), sum(record['score'] for record in loaded))
print('resources closed')

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: JSON parsing does not authorize a file path or make its contents safe to execute. The standard decoder accepts duplicate object names with a last-value policy; a strict ingestion pipeline should reject them explicitly when ambiguity matters. Treat malformed text, missing files, and wrong schemas as distinct errors. For important writes, design atomic replacement and backup policy separately from handle cleanup.

content_blocks.question: json.loads succeeds on a payload. What has this established?
options: The decoder accepted the syntax, not the application schema
The content is safe Python code
content_blocks.explanation: Syntax parsing creates Python values. Field types, required keys, ranges, and other application constraints still require validation.

content_blocks.question: An exception leaves `with path.open(...) as handle:`. What normally happens to the file handle?
options: It remains open until the next loop
It is automatically deleted from disk
content_blocks.explanation: The file context manager closes the resource on exit. Closing a handle is different from deleting the file or undoing writes.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: replace one score with true in JSON. Explain why a strict int check rejects it while isinstance(score, int) would not.
Modify: also require a nonblank string name and reject unknown record keys. Verify an empty list has a valid zero-total result.
Design: build a JSON report importer that validates the entire document before writing any destination file. Describe duplicate-key handling, encoding errors, and a no-partial-output failure policy.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

Does `with open(..., 'w')` guarantee a safe transactional write? Explain cleanup versus truncation, partial output, and atomic replacement. Then describe why schema validation must precede destructive operations.

content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-classes-and-state. Move repeated validation rules into an object whose methods preserve a clear invariant.

topics.title: Classes, Instance State, and Invariants
objectives: Distinguish class attributes from per-instance state
Design methods that preserve an invariant
Prefer composition when an object contains another object's responsibilities

subtopics.title: State and behavior can share a contract

content_blocks.value: Explanation: a class is more than a namespace

A class defines behavior for instances. Each ordinary instance can have its own attributes, while attributes defined on the class are shared through lookup. An __init__ method initializes a newly created instance; it is not the allocation operation itself. When a function defined on a class is accessed as an instance method, binding supplies the instance as self. This connects methods to the state they must preserve. An invariant such as a nonnegative balance should hold after initialization and after every supported operation.

Mechanism: place a fresh history list in __init__ so each ledger gets independent mutable state. Validate a deposit amount before changing either balance or history, avoiding half-applied operations for expected validation errors. The public method updates related state together. A leading underscore communicates an internal attribute by convention; it does not enforce a security boundary. Prefer composition when a report uses a ledger rather than claiming to be a ledger. Inheritance should reflect a substitutable behavior contract, not merely reuse a few methods.

content_blocks.title: Per-instance state and shared behavior
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    Class[Ledger class methods] --> First[First ledger instance]
    Class --> Second[Second ledger instance]
    First --> HistoryA[Fresh history A]
    Second --> HistoryB[Fresh history B]
Worked example: independent ledgers and rejected changes

Two ledgers start with independent history lists. Depositing into the first does not change the second. A negative deposit raises before any state update, so the first ledger still has its original valid balance and one history entry. The example uses integer credits rather than floating-point money, keeping numeric representation separate from the object-state lesson.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: A history = [] class attribute would be shared until an instance shadows it; appending through an instance would mutate that shared list. A class does not automatically prevent callers from editing public attributes. Properties or a narrower interface can improve discipline, but process isolation and validation are still needed at trust boundaries. Use a simple function when there is no persistent state to manage.

content_blocks.question: Where should a fresh mutable history list be assigned to avoid sharing it across Ledger instances?
options: As history = [] in the class body
content_blocks.explanation: Each __init__ call evaluates a new list expression and binds it on that instance. The other choices share a definition-time object.

content_blocks.question: Why validate a deposit before updating balance?
options: To preserve state when a validation failure occurs
content_blocks.explanation: Rejecting before mutation keeps the previous valid state for expected invalid inputs. This alone does not provide concurrency safety.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: move history into the class body and deposit into both instances. Identify which printed values reveal shared state.
Modify: add withdraw with validation for positive integers and sufficient balance. Prove that a rejected withdrawal changes neither balance nor history.
Design: create a report object that holds a Ledger and formats a read-only summary. Explain why composition is more accurate than inheriting Ledger just to call its methods.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

What is the difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute when both have the same name? Explain lookup, shadowing, and mutation of a shared object. Discuss why underscore naming is a convention rather than enforced privacy.

content_blocks.value: Continue to python-foundations-modules-and-testing. Verify object invariants and pure functions through repeatable tests rather than manual demonstrations alone.

topics.title: Modules, Testable Design, and a Report Capstone
objectives: Separate importable computation from command-line side effects
Test empty, boundary, tie, and invalid-input cases
Explain why annotations and examples are not runtime validation

subtopics.title: Make importing safe and correctness repeatable

content_blocks.value: Explanation: a module is also executable code

A module groups definitions and has a namespace, but its top-level statements execute when it is first imported in a process. Normal repeated imports reuse the cached module; that is not a reason to put network writes or input prompts at import time. Place command-line orchestration in a main function behind an `if __name__ == '__main__'` guard. Keep core computation callable without stdin, filesystem access, or printing. This makes both reuse and automated verification straightforward.

Mechanism: a test supplies an input and checks an observable contract using assertions that the test framework reports. Partition the behavior into empty input, typical input, boundary scores, stable ties, and invalid data. A successful example is one observation, not proof across all inputs. Type annotations describe intent for tools but do not enforce validation automatically. In the capstone, ranking checks each integer score before sorting, creates a fresh result, and defines ties by stable input order. Test failure paths and unchanged inputs as deliberately as happy-path output.

content_blocks.title: Separate the entry point from the tested core
content_blocks.value:
flowchart LR
    CLI[CLI parsing] --> Core[Validated ranking function]
    Tests[Tests with explicit cases] --> Core
    Core --> Data[Returned records]
    Data --> Display[CLI formatting]
Worked example: a tiny deterministic verification harness

A unittest case verifies that ties preserve input order, an empty input returns an empty list, an invalid score raises, and the original records remain unchanged. The harness reports only a stable pass/fail count instead of elapsed-time text. In a real module, the function would be imported by the tests, and input parsing would live in a guarded entry point. The checks here run only as a trusted authored example, not as a service endpoint for arbitrary code.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and tradeoffs
content_blocks.value: A file named json.py can shadow the standard library module. Test fixtures should not depend on mutable global state or execution order. Do not use eval to parse a report. A pure core still needs a well-defined input contract: this example expects a reusable sequence of two-field records, not a one-shot iterator that validation would exhaust before sorting.

content_blocks.question: Which placement prevents a CLI input prompt from running during normal import?
options: At module top level before imports
Inside main called only under the __main__ guard
content_blocks.explanation: The guard is false for a normal import, so main's command-line side effects are not invoked.

content_blocks.question: A score parameter is annotated int. Does that automatically reject a runtime string argument?
options: Only when the string contains digits
No, explicit validation or a separate runtime validator is needed
content_blocks.explanation: Ordinary function annotations are not automatic runtime checks. The contract must be enforced where the application requires it.

content_blocks.value: Progressive practice

items: Predict: import a module that prints at top level twice in one process. Contrast normal cached imports with executing its guarded CLI entry point.
Modify: add explicit record-shape and nonblank-name validation to rank_scores, then test each rejected shape without relying on incidental exceptions.

Design: assemble a stdin JSON ranking program using separate parse, validate, rank, and format functions. Reject the entire batch on invalid input, preserve stable ties, and cover empty input, booleans, range boundaries, and no input mutation.

content_blocks.value: Interview question

How would you turn a working script into a maintainable library plus CLI? Explain import side effects, a pure computation boundary, explicit validation, and deterministic tests. Give a failure case that a single sample output would not reveal.
